before.title: Nonzero cell heads classify the simple modules of a cellular algebra
before.strategy: Follow Graham-Lehrer. (a) If $x\in C^{\lambda}\setminus\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}$ then after scaling $\langle x,y\rangle=1$ for some $y$; the elements built from $y$ and the cellular basis send the image of $x$ to every basis vector of the quotient, so every nonzero submodule of $D^{\lambda}$ is everything (Proposition 2.9); the computation is field-independent, giving absolute simplicity. (b) Any nonzero homomorphism $C^{\mu}\to C^{\lambda}$ forces comparability of $\mu,\lambda$ in $\Lambda$ (Proposition 2.10), whence distinct nonzero heads are non-isomorphic (Corollary 2.11). (c) For exhaustion, filter $A$ by the two-sided ideals $A^{\unrhd\lambda}$ for a linear extension of $\Lambda$; each successive quotient is a cell module, so every simple $A$-module is a composition factor of some $C^{\lambda}$; induction on $\lambda$, using that the composition factors of $\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}$ occur among the $D^{\mu}$ with $\mu\rhd\lambda$ (the description of the radical in the proof of Theorem 2.13), reduces every simple factor to a nonzero $D^{\mu}$. Finally $\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}=C^{\lambda}$ exactly when the form is identically zero. This is Mathas, Theorem 2.13 with Propositions 2.9-2.12; no choice is used.

after.title: Nonzero cell heads classify the simple modules of a cellular algebra
after.strategy:
Use the right-cell action identity $xC^{\lambda}_{uv}=\langle x,c^{\lambda}_uangle_\lambda c^{\lambda}_v$, obtained directly by comparing the cellular product modulo $A^{hd\lambda}$. The form radical is a submodule by [[lem-cell-form-is-associative-and-its-radical-is-a-submodule]]. If $x$ lies outside it, choose $y=\sum_u a_uc^{\lambda}_u$ with $\langle x,yangle_\lambda=1$ and put $b_v=\sum_u a_uC^{\lambda}_{uv}$. Then $xb_v=c^{\lambda}_v$ for every $v$. Thus every vector outside the form radical generates the entire cell module; every proper submodule lies in that radical. When the form is not identically zero, the radical is therefore the unique maximal proper submodule, the quotient is simple, and the radical equals the module Jacobson radical. The same rank-one computation after any field extension, together with base change of the kernel of a finite Gram matrix, proves absolute simplicity. A form is not identically zero exactly when its radical is proper, exactly when this quotient is nonzero; nondegeneracy of the original form instead means its radical is zero.
For distinctness, let $A^{\unrhd
u}$ be the span of cells with labels at least $
u$. These are two-sided ideals by the cellular axioms and the anti-involution. A product of a $\lambda$-cell basis element and a $
u$-cell basis element lies in both upward-cell ideals. If $\lambda$ does not dominate $
u$, all labels in their intersection are strictly above $\lambda$, so the $
u$-cell basis elements act as zero on $C^{\lambda}$. In contrast the $\lambda$-cell elements act nontrivially on $D^{\lambda}$ when its form is nonzero, by the rank-one identity. If $D^{\lambda}\cong D^{\mu}
e0$, comparison of these actions forces both $\lambda\unrhd\mu$ and $\mu\unrhd\lambda$, hence $\lambda=\mu$.
For completeness choose a linear extension listing larger cells first and let $0=I_0\subset I_1\subset\cdots\subset I_N=A$ be the corresponding upward-closed cellular ideals. If $\lambda$ is the newly added label at stage $j$, the right $A$-module $I_j/I_{j-1}$ is the direct sum of $|T(\lambda)|$ copies of $C^{\lambda}$, with the first basis index fixed in each copy. For any simple right module $S$, take the least $j$ with $SI_j
e0$. Then $SI_j=S$ and $SI_{j-1}=0$. For some $s\in S$ the map $I_j/I_{j-1}	o S$, $a+I_{j-1}\mapsto sa$, is nonzero, so its restriction to one cell-module copy surjects onto $S$. If the $\lambda$-form were zero, the cellular multiplication rule would give $I_j^2\subset I_{j-1}$, contradicting $SI_j^2=(SI_j)I_j=S$. Its form is therefore nonzero and the already proved uniqueness of the maximal proper submodule forces $S\cong D^{\lambda}$. This proves exhaustion without an unsupported radical-factor induction. All sets and linear extensions are finite and no choice principle is used. before.title: Cellular decomposition matrices are unitriangular for the cell order
before.strategy: If $d_{\lambda\mu}\ne0$ then there are a submodule $M\subseteq C^{\lambda}$ and a surjection $C^{\mu}\to C^{\lambda}/M$ with image $D^{\mu}$; composing with the projection onto the head produces a nonzero homomorphism $C^{\mu}\to C^{\lambda}$ modulo submodules supported on strictly smaller cells, and Proposition 2.10(i) forces $\lambda\unrhd\mu$. For $\lambda=\mu$ the radical of $C^{\mu}$ is its unique maximal submodule (Theorem 2.13), so $d_{\mu\mu}=1$. This is Mathas, Corollary 2.14; no choice is used.

after.title: Cellular decomposition matrices are unitriangular for the cell order
after.strategy: The cellular multiplication rule and the two upward-cell ideals show that every $\mu$-cell basis element acts as zero on $C^{\lambda}$ if $\lambda$ does not dominate $\mu$. It consequently acts as zero on every subquotient, while the rank-one formula shows that these elements act nontrivially on nonzero $D^{\mu}$. Hence $d_{\lambda\mu}\ne0$ implies $\lambda\unrhd\mu$. For the diagonal, the $\mu$-cell basis elements annihilate the form radical of $C^{\mu}$ by the same rank-one formula, and act nontrivially on $D^{\mu}$. Thus no composition factor of that radical is $D^{\mu}$, whereas the quotient by it is exactly one copy of $D^{\mu}$ by [[thm-nonzero-cell-heads-classify-the-simple-modules-of-a-cellular-algebra]]. Additivity of finite composition multiplicities gives $d_{\mu\mu}=1$. Listing larger labels first puts allowed entries below the labelled diagonal, giving the stated rectangular lower-unitriangular matrix. This replaces the unsupported subquotient-lifting argument; no choice is used.

before.title: Cellularity does not make every cell module simple
before.statement: A cellular algebra need not be semisimple, its cell modules need not be simple, and a labelled head $D^{\lambda}$ may vanish although the cell module $C^{\lambda}$ is nonzero. (a) Abstract degenerate instance: let $F$ be a field and $A=F[x]/(x^2)$, with $\Lambda=\{1\rhd2\}$ ordered so that $1\rhd2$, cellular basis $c_{11}:=1$ in cell $1$ and $c_{22}:=x$ in cell $2$ and $i=\mathrm{id}$ ([[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]]). The triangular axiom holds because $1\cdot a\equiv0\bmod(x)$ for $a\in(x)$ and $x\cdot a\in\{x,0\}$, and $A^{\rhd2}=0$. The cell form on $C^{2}$ has $c_{22}c_{22}=x^2=0$, so it is identically zero, $\mathrm{rad}\,C^{2}=C^{2}$ and $D^{2}=0$, while $C^{1}\cong F$ is simple: cellularity does not force $D^{\lambda}\ne0$, and the algebra is not semisimple since $\mathrm{rad}\,A=(x)$. (b) Hecke instance: let $F$ be a field of characteristic $2$ and $q=1$, so $e=\operatorname{char}(F)=2$ ([[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]]); for $n=3$ and $\lambda=(1,1,1)$ the partition $(1,1,1)$ is not $2$-regular ([[def-e-regular-and-e-restricted-partitions]]), so $D^{(1,1,1)}=0$ while the page's Specht module $S^{(1,1,1)}\cong D^{(3)}$ is the nonzero trivial module (in characteristic $2$ the sign module is trivial) ([[thm-simple-type-a-hecke-modules-are-indexed-by-e-regular-partitions]], [[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]). (c) Reducible cell module: at $e=2$ the q-Schur cell module $W^{(3,2)}_F$ satisfies $\sum_{i>0}[W^{(3,2)}_F(i)]=[L^{(3,1^2)}_F]+2[L^{(2^2,1)}_F]\ne0$ ([[thm-q-schaper-virtual-radical-layer-formula]], the calculation of [[ex-q-schaper-for-shape-three-two-at-e-two]]), so its radical is nonzero and $W^{(3,2)}_F$ is reducible even though it has a simple head.
before.strategy: Part (a) is a direct computation in the two-dimensional algebra $F[x]/(x^2)$: every product of two elements of the smaller cell vanishes. Part (b) reads the $2$-regularity of $(1,1,1)$ off the definition and applies the classification theorem; the cell module $S^{(1^3)}$ at $q=1$ is the sign module, which is the trivial module in characteristic $2$. Part (c) is the Weyl-module computation of Example 5.33, where the Jantzen layers have positive dimension. All three instances are applications of [[thm-nonzero-cell-heads-classify-the-simple-modules-of-a-cellular-algebra]], whose third clause says that $D^{\lambda}\ne0$ holds exactly when the cell form is non-degenerate. No choice is used.

after.title: Cellularity does not make every cell module simple
after.statement: A cellular algebra need not be semisimple, its cell modules need not be simple, and a labelled cell-form quotient $D^{\lambda}$ may vanish although the cell module $C^{\lambda}$ is nonzero. (a) Abstract degenerate instance: let $F$ be a field and $A=F[x]/(x^2)$, with $\Lambda=\{2\rhd1\}$ ordered so that $2\rhd1$, cellular basis $c_{11}:=1$ in cell $1$ and $c_{22}:=x$ in cell $2$ and $i=\mathrm{id}$ ([[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]]). The cell form on $C^{2}$ has $c_{22}c_{22}=x^2=0$, so it is identically zero, $\mathrm{rad}\,C^{2}=C^{2}$ and $D^{2}=0$, while both $C^{1}$ and $C^{2}$ are one-dimensional simple modules: on either, $a+bx$ acts as the scalar $a$. In particular the Jacobson radical of $C^{2}$ is zero and its actual head is $C^{2}$, even though its cell-form radical is all of $C^{2}$ and its cell-form quotient is zero: cellularity does not force $D^{\lambda}\ne0$, and the algebra is not semisimple since $\mathrm{rad}\,A=(x)$. (c) Reducible cell module: at $e=2$ the q-Schur cell module $W^{(3,2)}_F$ satisfies $\sum_{i>0}[W^{(3,2)}_F(i)]=[L^{(3,1^2)}_F]+2[L^{(2^2,1)}_F]\ne0$ ([[thm-q-schaper-virtual-radical-layer-formula]], the calculation of [[ex-q-schaper-for-shape-three-two-at-e-two]]), so its radical is nonzero and $W^{(3,2)}_F$ is reducible even though it has a simple head.

before.title: The Schur functor sends Weyl and simple modules to Specht and Hecke simple modules
before.strategy: By the definition of $\varphi_{ST}$, multiplying by $\varphi_{t^{\omega}t^{\omega}}$ kills all semistandard basis elements whose type is not $\omega$, and for type $\omega$ the surviving elements are exactly the $\varphi_t$ with $t$ a standard $\lambda$-tableau; this identifies the corner $W^{\lambda}e$ with the free module on the Murphy basis of the Hecke cell module $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm{M}}$, proving (1) for Weyl modules. Passing to heads and using that $F$ is exact ([[def-schur-idempotent-and-schur-functor-for-type-a-q-schur-algebras]]) and sends the head of $W^{\lambda}$ to the head of $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm{M}}$ gives $F(L^{\lambda})\cong D^{\lambda}_{\mathrm{M}}$, which is nonzero exactly when $\lambda$ is $e$-restricted by Theorem 3.39, proving (2). Part (3) follows by applying the exact functor to a composition series of $W^{\lambda}$ and using (1)-(2) termwise, the multiplicities of the $D^{\nu}_{\mathrm{M}}$ with $\nu$ $e$-restricted being preserved. This is Mathas, Proposition 4.19 with the printed p. 25 convention warning; the Dipper-James translation is Kleshchev's Remark 5.5. No choice is used.

after.title: The Schur functor sends Weyl and simple modules to Specht and Hecke simple modules
after.strategy: By the definition of $\varphi_{ST}$, multiplying by $\varphi_{t^{\omega}t^{\omega}}$ kills all semistandard basis elements whose type is not $\omega$, and for type $\omega$ the surviving elements are exactly the $\varphi_t$ with $t$ a standard $\lambda$-tableau; this identifies the corner $W^{\lambda}e$ with the free module on the Murphy basis of the Hecke cell module $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm{M}}$, proving (1) for Weyl modules. To identify the simple image, compare the cellular forms rather than assuming exactness preserves heads. The corner idempotent $e=\varphi_{t^{\omega}t^{\omega}}$ satisfies $e^*=e$. The semistandard product $\varphi_{T^{\lambda},s}\varphi_{t,T^{\lambda}}$, evaluated at $m_{\lambda}$, is the Murphy product $m_{t^{\lambda},s}m_{t,t^{\lambda}}$; higher Schur shapes evaluate to higher Murphy shapes. Its scalar coefficient therefore identifies the form on $W^{\lambda}e$ with the cell form on $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$. Associativity and $e^*=e$ make $W^{\lambda}e$ orthogonal to $W^{\lambda}(1-e)$, so $\mathrm{rad}(W^{\lambda})e=\mathrm{rad}(W^{\lambda}e)$. The Weyl form is nonzero because its canonical semistandard projection has Gram value $1$, and the repaired cellular classification identifies $L^{\lambda}=W^{\lambda}/\mathrm{rad}(W^{\lambda})$. Exactness now gives $F(L^{\lambda})\cong S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}/\mathrm{rad}(S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M})=D^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$, including the zero-form case. This quotient is nonzero exactly for the restricted shapes by Theorem 3.39; only then is it the actual Specht-module head. This proves (2). Part (3) follows by applying the exact functor to a composition series of $W^{\lambda}$ and using (1)-(2) termwise, the multiplicities of the $D^{\nu}_{\mathrm{M}}$ with $\nu$ $e$-restricted being preserved. This is Mathas, Proposition 4.19 with the signed convention made explicit above: $F(W^{\lambda'})=S^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M}=(S^{\lambda})^{\theta}$ and $F(L^{\lambda'})=D^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M}=(D^{\lambda})^{\theta}$. Applying the same involutive exact pullback to both modules preserves all composition multiplicities. The untwisted printedp25 warning is not used. No choice is used.

before.title: The type-A Hecke Specht module and its cell form
before.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring and $q\in R^{\times}$. With the Murphy cellular basis $(\mathcal M,\Lambda)$ of $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$ ([[thm-murphy-tableau-elements-form-a-cellular-basis]], [[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]]) and the canonical tableau $t^\lambda$ of shape $\lambda\vdash n$ ([[def-murphy-elements-and-murphy-tableau-elements]]), the **Murphy cell module** $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ is the right cell module $C^{\lambda}$ of the Murphy basis: it is the free $R$-module with basis $\{m_t:=m_{t^\lambda t}:t\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)\}$ - the classes of the Murphy elements whose *first* index is the canonical tableau - and $H$ acts by $m_th=\sum_vr_vm_v$ whenever $m_{t^\lambda t}h\equiv\sum_vr_vm_{t^\lambda v}\pmod{H^{\rhd\lambda}}$. (The cellular action rule transforms the second index and fixes the first, so the diagonal elements $m_{tt}$ alone do not span a submodule; the explicit failure for $\lambda=(2,1)$ is recorded in the proof strategy.) Its **cell form** is the unique bilinear form $\langle\ ,\ \rangle_\lambda:S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}\times S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}\to R$ with $$m_{us}m_{tv}\equiv\langle m_s,m_t\rangle_\lambda\,m_{uv}\pmod{H^{\rhd\lambda}}$$ for all $s,t,u,v\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)$; it is symmetric and associative and $\mathrm{rad}\,S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ is a submodule, so $D^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}:=S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}/\mathrm{rad}\,S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ is a right $H$-module ([[lem-cell-form-is-associative-and-its-radical-is-a-submodule]]).

**Convention (Dipper-James).** This page uses the Dipper-James Specht convention, in which the simple labels are the $e$-regular partitions: the page's **Specht module** $S^{\lambda}$ is the Dipper-James Specht module, while the source's Murphy cell module of the conjugate shape is its dual, $S^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M}$ being the dual of $S^{\lambda}$ (source, printed p. 25). Consequently every source statement phrased for $e$-restricted labels is translated on this page by conjugating partitions and dualising, using [[prop-p-regular-and-p-restricted-simple-labels-are-related-by-conjugate-sign-duality]] and the dictionary $D^{\mu}\cong D(\mu^{\mathrm{t}})\otimes\operatorname{sgn}$ of Kleshchev's Remark 5.5, whereas the Jucys-Murphy and seminormal theory is stated on this page for the Murphy cell module $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ itself. No semisimplicity is assumed and no choice principle is used.
before.strategy: A definition item: instantiate the general cell-module and cell-form construction at the Murphy basis, and record the conjugation/duality dictionary explicitly so that no later item silently mixes the two conventions. The cellular rule of [[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]] transforms the second index while fixing the first, so the module basis is indexed by the second index of the Murphy elements with the canonical tableau in the first index, $m_t=m_{t^\lambda t}$; the diagonal elements $m_{tt}$ alone are not closed under right multiplication: for $\lambda=(2,1)$ and $q=1$ one has $m_{uu}=1+(13)\notin m_{(2,1)}\mathbb Z[S_3]$, the right ideal generated by $m_{(2,1)}=1+(12)$ being spanned by $1+(12)$, $(23)+(123)$ and $(132)+(13)$, while the classes of $m_{t^\lambda t}=m_\lambda T_{d(t)}$ do span the cell module (the same pattern holds for $\lambda=(3,1)$). The properties of the form are [[lem-cell-form-is-associative-and-its-radical-is-a-submodule]]; the dictionary is the printed p. 25 warning of the source together with Kleshchev's Remark 5.5, cross-checked against the Murphy-basis normalisation of Hu-Mathas (Proposition 3.17). No choice is used.

after.title: The type-A Hecke Specht module and its cell form
after.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring and $q\in R^{\times}$. With the Murphy cellular basis $(\mathcal M,\Lambda)$ of $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$ ([[thm-murphy-tableau-elements-form-a-cellular-basis]], [[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]]) and the canonical tableau $t^\lambda$ of shape $\lambda\vdash n$ ([[def-murphy-elements-and-murphy-tableau-elements]]), the **Murphy cell module** $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ is the right cell module $C^{\lambda}$ of the Murphy basis: it is the free $R$-module with basis $\{m_t:=m_{t^\lambda t}:t\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)\}$ - the classes of the Murphy elements whose *first* index is the canonical tableau - and $H$ acts by $m_th=\sum_vr_vm_v$ whenever $m_{t^\lambda t}h\equiv\sum_vr_vm_{t^\lambda v}\pmod{H^{\rhd\lambda}}$. (The cellular action rule transforms the second index and fixes the first, so the diagonal elements $m_{tt}$ alone do not span a submodule; the explicit failure for $\lambda=(2,1)$ is recorded in the proof strategy.) Its **cell form** is the unique bilinear form $\langle\ ,\ \rangle_\lambda:S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}\times S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}\to R$ with $$m_{us}m_{tv}\equiv\langle m_s,m_t\rangle_\lambda\,m_{uv}\pmod{H^{\rhd\lambda}}$$ for all $s,t,u,v\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)$; it is symmetric and associative and $\mathrm{rad}\,S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ is a submodule, so $D^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}:=S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}/\mathrm{rad}\,S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ is a right $H$-module ([[lem-cell-form-is-associative-and-its-radical-is-a-submodule]]).

**Convention (Dipper-James signed cellular normalization).** Let $\theta:H\to H$ be the involutive algebra automorphism defined by $\theta(T_i)=-qT_i^{-1}=(q-1)-T_i$. For a right module $M$, write $M^\theta$ for the same $R$-module with action $x\cdot h=x\theta(h)$. The page's ordinary Specht normalization is the signed conjugate Murphy construction
$$S^{\lambda}:=(S^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M})^\theta.$$
Its form is the form of $S^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M}$ on the same underlying module; because $\theta$ commutes with $*$ this is associative for the twisted action. Over a field put
$$D^{\lambda}:=S^{\lambda}/\operatorname{rad}_{\rm form}S^{\lambda}=(D^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M})^\theta.$$
Thus $S^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M}=(S^{\lambda})^\theta$ and $D^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M}=(D^{\lambda})^\theta$; conjugation alone does not identify these modules. At $q=1$, $\theta(\sigma)=\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\sigma$, so these identities contain tensoring with sign. In characteristic $2$ the sign twist becomes trivial at $q=1$. The nonzero quotients in this signed normalization have $e$-regular labels because the nonzero Murphy quotients have conjugate $e$-restricted labels. No generic root-of-unity Hecke claim is inferred from the published prime-characteristic group-only sign dictionary. No semisimplicity or choice principle is assumed.
after.strategy: Keep the fixed-first-index Murphy-cell construction and its local product-defined form above. To check the signed normalization locally, the quadratic relation gives $T_i^{-1}=q^{-1}(T_i-(q-1))$. Therefore $\theta(T_i)=(q-1)-T_i$ exchanges the two roots $q$ and $-1$ of the quadratic relation. The inverses satisfy the commuting and braid relations, so the scalar multiples $-qT_i^{-1}$ do too; thus $\theta$ is an algebra homomorphism. Applying it twice fixes every generator and proves it is an involutive automorphism. Since $*$ fixes each $T_i$, $\theta$ commutes with the cellular anti-involution. Pullback along this automorphism preserves every submodule, quotient, exact sequence, simplicity and composition multiplicity, and twisting twice is identity. On $M^\theta$ the original form satisfies $\langle x\theta(h),y\rangle=\langle x,y\theta(h)^*\rangle=\langle x,y\theta(h^*)\rangle$, so its radical is unchanged as a subspace. Hence the stated $S$ and $D$ identities are literal consequences of the signed-cell definition, not of an unsupported assertion that taking duals conjugates a label. At $q=1$ all simple transpositions act after pullback with a minus sign, which proves the sign-twist interpretation. For $\lambda=(3)$ at $q=1$ in characteristic zero, $S_{\mathrm M}^{(1^3)}$ has $T_i=-1$; after twisting it has $T_i=1$ as ordinary $S^{(3)}$ must. before.statement: Let $F$ be a field, $q\in F^{\times}$, $e=e(F,q)$ and $H=H_{F,q}(S_n)$ ([[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]]). before.title: The q-Schaper virtual radical-layer formula
before.statement:
Let $R$ be a principal ideal domain, $\pi$ a prime element, $F=R/\pi R$ the residue field, and let $\hat q\in R^{	imes}$ satisfy $[n]!_{\hat q}
e0$ in $R$; put $q:=\hat q+\pi R\in F^{	imes}$. Let $d\ge1$, let $\lambda$ be a partition of $n$ with at most $d$ parts, and let $W^{\lambda}_F$ be the Weyl module of the q-Schur algebra $S_F(d,n)=S(d,n)\otimes_RF$ with its Jantzen filtration $W^{\lambda}_F(i)$ with respect to $(R,\pi)$ ([[def-jantzen-filtration-of-a-lifted-cell-module]], [[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]).
1. (**Jantzen sum formula**) In the Grothendieck group of finite-dimensional $S_F(d,n)$-modules, $$\sum_{i>0} igl[W^{\lambda}_F(i) igr]=\sum_{\substack{(a,b),(a,c)\in[\lambda]\ b<c}}\Bigl(
u_\pi igl([h^{\lambda}_{ab}]_{\hat q} igr)-
u_\pi igl([h^{\lambda}_{ac}]_{\hat q} igr)\Bigr)\Bigl[W_F^{( eta_1,\dots, eta_b+h^{\lambda}_{ab},\dots, eta_c-h^{\lambda}_{ac},\dots, eta_n)}\Bigr],$$ where $ eta= eta(\lambda)$ is the beta sequence of $\lambda$, $h^{\lambda}_{ab}$ are its hook lengths and the symbols are the virtual Weyl symbols of [[def-alternating-weyl-and-specht-symbols-from-beta-sequences]].
2. (**q-Schaper, $d\ge n$**) If $d\ge n$ and $\Pi$ denotes the Schur functor of [[def-schur-idempotent-and-schur-functor-for-type-a-q-schur-algebras]], then applying $\Pi$ to (1) gives the corresponding identity for the Hecke Specht modules in the source's normalisation, that is, for the Murphy cell modules $\Pi(W^{\lambda}_F)=S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ of [[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]] (the Dipper-James form is obtained by conjugating partitions), $$\sum_{i>0} igl[S^{\lambda}_F(i) igr]=\sum_{\substack{(a,b),(a,c)\in[\lambda]\ b<c}}\Bigl(
u_\pi igl([h^{\lambda}_{ab}]_{\hat q} igr)-
u_\pi igl([h^{\lambda}_{ac}]_{\hat q} igr)\Bigr)\Bigl[S_F^{( eta_1,\dots, eta_b+h^{\lambda}_{ab},\dots, eta_c-h^{\lambda}_{ac},\dots, eta_n)}\Bigr]$$ in the Grothendieck group of finite-dimensional $H_{F,q}(S_n)$-modules, with the virtual Specht symbols of [[def-alternating-weyl-and-specht-symbols-from-beta-sequences]]. The formula is a virtual radical-layer identity: each nonzero coefficient bounds the corresponding composition multiplicity from above and forces at least one occurrence of the corresponding simple factor, but it is not a general algorithm for decomposition numbers.
before.strategy:
For (1): by [[thm-q-schur-weyl-weight-space-gram-determinant-hook-product]] the Gram determinant on the $
u$-weight space is a product of hook ratios times $q^{N}$; the assumption $[n]!_{\hat q}
e0$ (with $R$ a domain) makes every factor nonzero, and by Jantzen's lemma ([[lem-jantzen-layer-dimensions-equal-the-gram-determinant-valuation]]) its $\pi$-valuation equals the total dimension of the positive Jantzen layers on that weight space. Taking $\pi$-adic valuations of the hook product turns each factor into the difference $
u_\pi([h^{\lambda}_{ab}]_{\hat q})-
u_\pi([h^{\lambda}_{ac}]_{\hat q})$, and Lemma 5.26 identifies the index of each term with the virtual Weyl symbol $[W_F^{( eta_1,\dots, eta_b+h^{\lambda}_{ab},\dots, eta_c-h^{\lambda}_{ac},\dots, eta_n)}]$ (here the hook-to-removable-border-strip correspondence [[lem-hooks-correspond-to-removable-border-strips]] is used). The resulting identities hold for every weight $
u$, so the unitriangular detection lemma [[lem-semistandard-weight-dimensions-detect-virtual-weyl-classes]] upgrades them to an identity in the Grothendieck group, giving (1). For (2) apply the exact Schur functor: by [[thm-schur-functor-sends-weyl-and-simple-modules-to-specht-and-hecke-simple-modules]] it carries $W^{\lambda}_F(i)$ to $S^{\lambda}_F(i)$ and commutes with Grothendieck classes, so (1) transports termwise, the vanishing virtual symbols accounting for the zero terms. This is Mathas, Theorem 5.31 and Corollary 5.32 (q-Schaper), printed pp. 58-60; no choice is used.

references.title: Mathas, Iwahori-Hecke Algebras and Schur Algebras of the Symmetric Group, Theorem 5.31 (Jantzen sum formula) and Corollary 5.32 (q-Schaper theorem), printed pp. 58-60

before.title: The q-Schaper calculation for (3,2) at e = 2
before.statement:
Take $R=\mathbb C[\hat q]$, the prime element $\pi=1+\hat q$ (so that $F=\mathbb C$ and $q:=\hat q+\pi R$ specialises to $-1$, giving $e=2$), and $\lambda=(3,2)$, $n=5$. Evaluating the q-Schaper virtual sums ([[thm-q-schaper-virtual-radical-layer-formula]]) with the hook valuations $
u_\pi([2]_{\hat q})=
u_\pi([4]_{\hat q})=1$, $
u_\pi([3]_{\hat q})=
u_\pi([1]_{\hat q})=0$ gives, in the source's normalisation, $$\sum_{i>0} igl[W^{(3,2)}_F(i) igr]= igl[W^{(3,1^2)}_F igr]+ igl[W^{(2^2,1)}_F igr]- igl[W^{(1^5)}_F igr],\qquad \sum_{i>0} igl[S^{(3,2)}_F(i) igr]=2 igl[D^{(2^2,1)}_{\mathrm{M}} igr].$$ Further Jantzen calculations give $W^{(1^5)}_F=L^{(1^5)}_F$, $W^{(2^2,1)}_F=L^{(2^2,1)}_F$ and $W^{(3,1^2)}_F\sim L^{(3,1^2)}_F+L^{(2^2,1)}_F+L^{(1^5)}_F$, so at the level of the sum formula alone one gets $d_{(3,2),(3,1^2)}=1$ and only the bound $d_{(3,2),(2^2,1)}\in\{1,2\}$. The extra dimension/filtration argument on the Specht side gives $S^{(3,2)}_{\mathrm{M}}\cong D^{(2^2,1)}_{\mathrm{M}}$ (both sides have dimension $5$), whence $d_{(3,2),(2^2,1)}=1$: the virtual sum alone did not determine the entry. Translated to the Dipper-James convention of this page by conjugating and dualising ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]), this reads $S^{(2,2,1)}_{\mathrm{DJ}}\cong D^{(3,2)}_{\mathrm{DJ}}$, while the partition $(2,2,1)$ is not $2$-regular, so its own labelled head vanishes, $D^{(2,2,1)}_{\mathrm{DJ}}=0$. The computed entry is consistent with the dominance bound $d_{\lambda\mu}
e0\Rightarrow\mu\unrhd\lambda$ of [[cor-type-a-hecke-decomposition-matrix-is-dominance-unitriangular]].
before.strategy: Compute $\nu_\pi$ on the quantum hook lengths ($[k]_{\hat q}$ is divisible by $\pi=1+\hat q$ exactly when $k$ is even), use the evaluation of the $(3,2)$ Gram determinant displayed in Example 5.28, and read off the virtual sums; the small-module equalities and the final dimension count are Example 5.33 of the source, including its closing remark that $d_{(3,2),(2^2,1)}$ is determined only after the extra argument. The translation to the page's convention is the conjugate-dual dictionary of [[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]. No choice is used.
